summary: This RFC proposes the Loader Debugger Protocol, an application protocol for loading, dumping, and debugging a target machine from a host over a network. It was an experimental proposal that asked for comments.

plainLanguage.summary: A bigger computer can put a program into a small one, look inside it, and fix problems, all over the network.

questions: what is the loader debugger protocol
how to load and debug remote machines over a network
what transport protocols does ldp use
subtitle: Remote machine loading, debugging, and control over the network.

tldr.problem: Developers need to load programs onto remote machines and debug them without physical access, but existing approaches are inefficient across heterogeneous machine types and network environments.
tldr.mechanism: LDP defines a layered protocol with five command classes (protocol, data transfer, control, management, and breakpoint) that work over a reliable transport (RDP or TCP) to provide loading, examination, modification, and debugging of remote systems.
tldr.outcome: The protocol never achieved widespread adoption, remaining experimental. It remains a historical example of how distributed debugging was approached in the 1980s ARPA environment.

facts.label: Command classes
facts.value: 6 (protocol, data transfer, control, management, breakpoint, condition)

today: RFC 909 is an Experimental protocol that was never widely adopted or standardized. It remains a historical artifact of 1980s debugging infrastructure, superseded by modern remote debugging protocols and tools.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Loader Debugger Protocol (LDP) is an application layer protocol for loading, dumping, and debugging target machines from a host across a network. The RFC specifies LDP as an experimental protocol that accommodates various processor types and operating systems while keeping complexity minimal for simpler implementations.

LDP is structured to support multiple use cases: full-featured debugging on capable systems, stripped-down loading and memory operations on resource-constrained devices like embedded loaders, and multi-user debugging of the same target. The protocol trades strict minimalism for feature richness, allowing both simple subset implementations and full-capability deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: LDP is a way for one computer to control another computer over a network: to put a program on it, read what is in its memory, change things, and fix problems.

sections.title: Protocol Overview and Architecture
sections.content:
An LDP session is an exchange of commands and responses between a host process (user, typically on a timesharing computer) and a target process (server, on the device being debugged like a gateway or packet switch). The host initiates and controls the session; the target is passive. A session starts when the host opens a transport connection and sends a HELLO command, which the target answers with HELLO_REPLY containing target capabilities, protocol version, system type, and address format. The session ends when the host closes the transport connection.

LDP runs on top of the Reliable Data Protocol (RDP, RFC 908) as the recommended transport, or TCP as a less-efficient alternative. It sits above the Internet Protocol (IP) in the network stack. The protocol uses implicit sequence numbers: each command sent from the host is implicitly numbered starting at zero and incrementing by one, saving space in message headers. The SYNCH command lets the host resynchronize if needed.

The protocol defines three implementation levels. LOADER_DUMPER provides only loading and memory operations. BASIC_DEBUGGER adds control commands for execution flow but not advanced breakpoints. FULL_DEBUGGER implements the complete protocol including conditional breakpoints and watchpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: The host (a big computer) opens a phone call to the target (a small device), says hello, learns what the target can do, then sends commands. The target listens and answers. When the host hangs up, the call is over.

sections.title: Command Classes and Structure
sections.content:
LDP commands are grouped into six classes identified by a command class code in the message header. Each command has a fixed two-word (32-bit) header containing the command length in octets and a class-type code. Commands must contain an even number of octets, so those with odd data lengths are padded.

The six command classes are: PROTOCOL (verification and error handling, including HELLO, SYNCH, ABORT, ERROR), DATA_TRANSFER (READ, WRITE, MOVE for memory and data operations), CONTROL (START, STOP, CONTINUE, STEP, REPORT for execution flow), MANAGEMENT (create, delete, list processes and breakpoints), BREAKPOINT (configure and run breakpoints on the target), and CONDITION (set conditional logic for breakpoints). User-specific commands can be defined in reserved codes above 63.

Data packing follows a uniform convention: most significant bit first, in order of increasing target address, into octets. Targets with non-standard word lengths (like 20-bit machines) pack multiple words into octets in a defined format to fit their address unit size.
sections.plainLanguage: Commands come in six flavors: hello and error messages, read and write data, start and stop execution, create and delete things, set breakpoints, and add conditions. Each command has a label at the start that says what it is and how long it is.

sections.title: Data Transfer Operations
sections.content:
Data transfer commands let the host examine and modify memory and other storage on the target. The READ command asks the target to read data from a specified address and return it in a READ_DATA response. The WRITE command deposits data at an address. The MOVE command copies data from one address range to another on the target, useful for initializing memory regions. Optional WRITE_MASK lets the host write to only certain bits, preserving others.

Commands specify an address using one of several addressing modes: long address format (for the full memory space) and short address format (for efficiency). Address modes can be absolute (a physical address), relative (offset from current address), or indirect (address from a register). The target reports available addressing modes in the HELLO_REPLY, and the choice depends on the target's hardware capabilities and the current task.

Data operations support repeating patterns through the REPEAT_DATA command, allowing the host to fill memory regions efficiently. All data transfer ensures alignment to the target's natural word size.
sections.plainLanguage: The host can ask the target: What is in memory at address X? (READ) or Put this data at address Y. (WRITE) The host can also ask the target to copy data from one place to another, or fill memory with a pattern.

sections.title: Control and Debugging
sections.content:
Control commands let the host run and pause code on the target. START tells the target to begin execution (or continue after a breakpoint). STOP pauses execution, CONTINUE resumes from where it stopped, and STEP executes a single instruction. The target sends an EXCEPTION message back to the host when a breakpoint is hit or execution stops, allowing the host to inspect state and decide the next action.

Management commands create and delete runtime objects: processes, breakpoints, and named memory regions. CREATE specifies which kind of object to create and passes initial parameters; CREATE_DONE confirms success and returns an object identifier. DELETE removes objects by identifier. LIST commands query what processes, breakpoints, and memory regions exist, returning address lists and process identifiers.

Breakpoints and watchpoints run on the target machine itself, not in the debugger. This is critical for real-time systems: the target's application code continues at full speed between breakpoint hits. Each breakpoint can have conditional commands (count triggers, value changes, comparisons) evaluated on the target, reducing the volume of data sent to the host. The BREAKPOINT_DATA command configures complex conditional logic using chained conditions and state changes, making LDP suitable for sophisticated, non-intrusive debugging of production systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The host can start a program on the target, pause it, step through one instruction at a time, and check what it is doing. The host can also tell the target: Stop when you reach this address or Stop when this variable changes. The target checks those conditions itself, so the program keeps running fast.
